name: Daria Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a usual workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the horn section in a regional concert band, record slow entries and teach two serious students. I have a master's degree in music and have spent thirty years getting a brass section to arrive together after a long rest. I still like the feel of cold metal warming in my hands before the first note.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do the band calls fit home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner runs steady shifts at a postal depot and our children are grown. We rent and have five months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for a senior player, and a few other bands are within a bus journey, though I have no offer from them. I use AI occasionally for draft travel times after another player tests a tool, then check the paper call sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that a quicker travel list is useful if the paid call and hall address remain on it. A horn player still has to follow the conductor’s hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five months saved and my partner's regular wage can cover one delayed concert fee. The band has a signed season, so I expect mild AI to leave my playing and lessons in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll check seven paid calls and two students against the signed season and ask for a written cancellation rate. In the first year of this mild change I'll keep checking occasional AI travel drafts against the paper call and save a sixth of any extra cleared concert fee after rent, food and horn maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the dates already signed. One late fee would be inconvenient, but it would not put rent in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a hall changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A council hall changed an evening show last winter. The band received a rehearsal fee, and the written cancellation term covered half the performance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the journey?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the hall entrance and last bus on paper before telling the younger horns when to arrive. An AI travel list with the wrong hall address is still wrong however fast it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the band treasurer whether generated slow-entry tracks will replace the small recordings it pays me to make. I'd ask for the live section-leading fee to stay separate from track pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tracks bring about one eighth of my own pay. Losing them would be real, but five months saved and a few nearby bands mean I can search before changing the household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll total a year's track invoices and ask the treasurer for the next six months of signed paid calls. In the first year, if track orders fall, I'll offer a paid live warm-up for our younger horns only when the band books it at a written rate outside my current paid calls; I won't buy an unproven AI recording tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic cut to recording fees. A suggestion from the treasurer is not a booked hour.

transcript.text: Is the live warm-up booked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the treasurer has not agreed to that warm-up. I would not put it into our income list until a fee and date are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a new AI recording tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trusted player can show me a tool on music they own, but not on students' audio without written permission. I would need a paid-use licence, local storage and manual checks before any trial of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that thinking AGI by 2028 could make slow horn entries before a robot plays horn. Playing robots follow around 2031, and I would get the live dates signed now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the track orders to end in 2028, costing an eighth of my pay. I do not expect the signed live band season to vanish at once, but I would need replacement work if it did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll count track income, request the next signed paid band dates and get an actual pension estimate before discussing a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid brass-section coach role only if my master's and section-leading experience meet its requirements, live human section coaching is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the last bus works; I'll keep band and students until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the expected track loss even with five months saved. A live-call collapse would be a larger conditional problem, not my current forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a coaching post open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No college has offered me a coaching post. I would check a current paid posting and actual rehearsal duties before moving a band call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen a pension estimate. Five months saved do not tell me what a pension would pay for years of rent.

Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.text: I'd tell the memorial hall that five years to AGI by 2031 gives me time to offer a separate paid horn service for families who ask for live music. Playing robots follow around 2034, but I would quote a fee before holding a Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may remove the small practice tracks before 2031. A memorial service could add income if a hall really books it, but I will not use our rent reserve to wait for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll give a local memorial hall a written price for a separate live horn service only if it books a real paid date, covers my playing, preparation and bus fare, confirms in writing that it provides a suitable safe room, and does not displace band or student calls. In the first year after 2031, if track fees have ended, I'll keep offering the service only while those signed paid and room terms hold; with no booking I'll keep current band and teaching work and put no memorial fee in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing track pay, though a paid second buyer could help. A bereaved family asking about a horn tune is not a paid memorial booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the memorial hall booked you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No memorial hall has signed a date. Someone asked the price, and I gave a price, not a promise of income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who provides the room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall must confirm in writing a safe space for a horn and the bus home. I won't pay room hire to perform a service it has not sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us read pension figures and paid band calls before setting a stopping date. Horn-playing robots follow around 2039, but rent will be due first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still want live band and teaching work. Five months saved helps now, but I do not know an actual pension amount that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid band schedule, then save a sixth of each extra cleared festival fee after rent, food and horn maintenance toward seven months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep booked paid band and student work and offer separate memorial services only with signed fees covering playing, preparation and bus, written safe-room provision and no clashes; if live band pay falls and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted paid brass-coach role only if my master's and section-leading qualify, live human section coaching is paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit, staying with current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about a decade away while the signed season and five-month reserve hold. A pension estimate will decide more than a calendar birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra festival fee clears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No extra festival call means no saving from that source. I will not move rent money to chase seven months on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen a pension statement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we do not have pension statements yet. I will read the actual payable amount against rent before giving up a paid date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because even the small practice-track fee could end before I know if band calls hold. Signed dates, actual pension figures and a posted qualified brass-coach role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the hall has sold a service before asking a musician to wait by the telephone. A quoted horn fee is not a booked memorial performance.

headlineQuote: A quoted horn fee is not a booked memorial performance.
portrait: Daria is a **58-year-old senior horn leader** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
Her **typical pay**, five-month reserve and some nearby bands provide a buffer against small recording losses.
She uses **AI occasionally** for travel drafts and checks them against paper calls.
She offers **separate memorial music** only on signed paid dates covering preparation, bus and a safe room.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end Daria's smaller practice-track fees before live calls are secure.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed band dates**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying live coaching with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
